blocks.text: 1. Semantic Chunking

blocks.alt: Sentences are measured for semantic similarity to produce coherent chunks

blocks.text: Semantic Chunking covers how meaning itself can guide where chunks are split, moving beyond structural boundaries entirely.
It cuts at points where the actual topic shifts, not just where structure allows.
2. Recursive Chunking's Blind Spot
As covered under still not fully semantic in Recursive Chunking, recursive chunking respects paragraphs and sentences, but two adjacent sentences can discuss completely different topics.
Semantic chunking was designed specifically to catch exactly that case.
3. Measuring Meaning Between Sentences

blocks.alt: Sentence 1 and sentence 2 produce a similarity score

blocks.text: As covered under retrieval using embeddings in What Is RAG, embedding each sentence lets similarity be measured between neighbors.
A large drop in similarity signals a topic shift.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal","What it suggests"],"rows":[["High similarity between neighbors","Same topic, keep in the same chunk"],["Low similarity between neighbors","Topic shift, a candidate chunk boundary"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Finding The Break Points

blocks.alt: A similarity drop causes a break point to be inserted

blocks.text: Scanning consecutive sentence similarity scores reveals where the biggest drops happen.
Those drop points become the candidate chunk boundaries.
5. Grouping Coherent Sentences

blocks.alt: Similar sentences get grouped into one chunk

blocks.text: Sentences between two break points share a consistent topic.
Grouping them together produces a chunk that reads as one coherent idea.
6. Computational Cost

blocks.alt: Recursive chunking is cheap while semantic chunking embeds every sentence

blocks.text: Embedding every sentence individually costs far more than a simple character count.
Semantic chunking trades away the speed and predictability covered in Fixed Chunking.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Semantic chunking requires an embedding call for every sentence before splitting even happens, meaning it is far slower and more expensive than fixed or recursive chunking on the same document.

blocks.text: 7. Higher Quality Chunk Boundaries
A chunk that stays on one topic embeds into a more focused, useful vector.
As covered under retrieval precision in Why Chunking, paying that extra cost buys sharper retrieval.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The tradeoff is direct: semantic chunking spends more compute upfront during ingestion so that every later retrieval query returns cleaner, more topically focused chunks.

blocks.text: 8. Choosing A Similarity Threshold

blocks.alt: A low threshold gives bigger chunks while a high threshold gives smaller chunks

blocks.text: Too sensitive a threshold creates too many tiny chunks; too loose a threshold misses real topic shifts.
Tuning that threshold is a practical, ongoing calibration step.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Threshold setting","Effect"],"rows":[["Too sensitive","Many small, overly fragmented chunks"],["Too loose","Real topic shifts get missed entirely"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Semantic Chunking Is Worth Its Extra Cost

blocks.alt: Needing the highest-quality boundaries points toward semantic chunking

blocks.text: Dense, topic varied documents benefit most from semantic chunking.
Already short or highly uniform content, by contrast, rarely needs semantic chunking's extra cost.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates finding a topic shift using sentence similarity.

code.content:
sentences = [
    "Machine learning models learn patterns from data.",
    "Training requires large datasets and significant compute.",
    "The company was founded in a small garage in 2010.",
    "It has since grown to over five hundred employees.",
]

def fake_sentence_embedding(sentence):
    # a simplified stand in for a real sentence embedding
    ml_words = {"machine", "learning", "models", "data", "training", "datasets", "compute"}
    words = set(sentence.lower().split())
    return len(words & ml_words)

def cosine_like_similarity(a, b):
    # a simplified stand in for real embedding similarity
    return 1.0 - abs(a - b) / max(a + b, 1)

embeddings = [fake_sentence_embedding(s) for s in sentences]
print("Sentence topic scores:", embeddings)

print("\nConsecutive similarity scores:")
for i in range(len(embeddings) - 1):
    sim = cosine_like_similarity(embeddings[i], embeddings[i + 1])
    marker = " <- topic shift" if sim < 0.5 else ""
    print(f"  Sentence {i} -> {i + 1}: similarity={sim:.2f}{marker}")

print("\nResulting chunks:")
print(f"  Chunk 0: {' '.join(sentences[:2])!r}")
print(f"  Chunk 1: {' '.join(sentences[2:])!r}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows similarity dropping sharply between the second and third sentences, exactly where the topic shifts from machine learning to company history, correctly triggering a chunk boundary at that point.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Using semantic chunking on every document without weighing its higher computational cost.
Setting a similarity threshold that is far too sensitive, producing tiny, fragmented chunks.
Setting a similarity threshold that is far too loose, missing real topic shifts entirely.
Forgetting that semantic chunking still needs a fallback size limit to avoid runaway large chunks.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Semantic chunking cuts at points where the actual topic shifts, not just where structure allows.
It addresses recursive chunking's blind spot, where adjacent sentences can differ completely in topic.
Embedding each sentence allows similarity to be measured between consecutive neighbors.
A large drop in similarity between neighboring sentences signals a candidate chunk boundary.
Sentences between two break points get grouped into one topically coherent chunk.
It costs far more computationally than fixed or recursive chunking, since every sentence needs embedding.
That extra cost buys sharper, more focused embeddings and better retrieval precision.
Choosing the right similarity threshold is a practical calibration step, balancing sensitivity and granularity.
